Investigating and Comparing the Perceptions of
Voice Interaction in Digital Games: Opportunities
for Health and Wellness Applications
V´ıtor Marques Carvalho
PPGIA
Universidade de Fortaleza
Fortaleza-CE, Brazil
vitor96mc@gmail.com
Maria Andr´eia Formico Rodrigues
PPGIA
Universidade de Fortaleza
Fortaleza-CE, Brazil
andreia.formico@gmail.com
Abstract—This study investigates and compares perceptions of
voice interaction in digital games, focusing on three scenarios:
game interacts with the player through voice, player interacts
with another player through voice, and player interacts with the
game through voice. We analyze the state-of-the-art, particularly
in AAA games, and conduct a comparative study involving game
expert participants from academia and industry, undergraduate
students, and generative AIs. The study aims to provide insights
to improve gameplay experiences, reduce disruptive behaviours,
and identify the influence of different voice interaction modalities
on player engagement, experience, motivations, and limitations
concerning current technology. Based on this comparative anal-<re>ysis, we expect to identify opportunities for enhancing voice
interaction in digital games, particularly in health and wellness
applications, and anticipate future trends in this field.
Index Terms—voice interaction, digital games, comparative
study, human and AI generative participants, health and wellness
I. INTRODUCTION
Voice interaction has long been a part of everyday life,
from basic phone calls to AI voice assistants [1]. The re-<re>cent pandemic further highlighted the importance of voice
interaction as leisure and work activities shifted to virtual
environments. This trend is particularly noticeable in digital
games in multiplayer genres, where voice communication is
crucial for team collaboration and achieving victory.
Voice interaction, in its most fundamental form, involves
human-to-human communication. However, digital games of-<re>ten employ voice interactions between player-controlled and
non-playable characters (NPCs). These dialogues create ex-<re>periences that closely resemble a human conversation. In
this context, virtual assistants can be compared to NPCs,
acting as conversational agents participating in dialogues to
exchange information [2]. In addition, when analyzing the
roles of characters, their functions in the narrative, and the
duality between playable and NPCs, it is possible to observe
an analogy between the player and an AI voice assistant,
which occurs when the voice assistant is compared to the
role of an NPC, a conversational agent who participates in

a dialogue to exchange information. This design approach can
be employed in game development, mechanics, and gameplay.
It is identified as a pattern of voice interaction, referred to
as unscripted conversation [3]. In scripted conversation, the
player formulates and verbalizes sentences personifying the
role of the main character. When there are no direct dialogues,
NPCs assume intelligent programming that may (or may not)
involve AI coded in their behaviour.
Despite its potential, voice interaction in digital games has
historically experienced ups and downs [4]. Early products
had limited command options and high error rates, resulting
in unsatisfactory user experiences. Furthermore, the number
of games utilizing voice interaction is scarce, and the tech-<re>nology often serves as an optional feature rather than the
main mode of interaction. Moreover, games that specifically
use voice interaction are even less common in the health
domain. While voice interaction has shown promise in certain
serious applications, such as assisting people with disabilities
or offering hands-free controls for medical professionals, its
implementation in health-related games is not yet widespread.
Currently, voice interaction is common in online and co-<re>operative games, facilitating communication between players
to coordinate strategies and achieve objectives. However, this
modality also poses challenges, such as microphone quality
and disruptive or toxic behaviour from certain players. This
can create an unhealthy and hostile environment, undermining
one of the fundamental pillars of gaming: to entertain [5].
The gaming industry has evolved significantly in recent
years, with voice interaction growing in digital games. The
release of ambitious AAA games [6] with large-scale budgets
and time investments has accompanied this growth. While
technology has faced challenges, it offers the potential to cre-<re>ate more immersive and engaging experiences with complex
and engaging narratives [7]. By understanding the history and
current state of voice interaction in gaming, researchers can
identify opportunities for improvement, especially in the health
and wellness fields.
This study examines perceptions of voice interaction in
digital games across three different scenarios: game interacts


with the player through voice, player interacts with another
player through voice, and player interacts with the game
through voice. We conduct a comparative study with expert
participants from the Brazilian digital gaming community,
undergraduate students, and generative AIs. The research
aims to provide insights to enhance gameplay experiences,
minimize disruptive behaviours, and assess the impact of voice
interaction scenarios on player engagement, motivations, and
limitations related to current technology. Our findings are ex-<re>pected to reveal opportunities for improving voice interaction
in digital games, including in health and wellness applications,
and forecast future trends in this domain. We sought and
obtained ethical approval from the Human Research Ethics
Committee to conduct this research. This approval, evidenced
by Certificate Number 67142923.4.0000.5052, ensured the
safety and privacy of our study’s participants while allowing us
to make meaningful advancements in voice interaction within
digital games.
II. AN OVERVIEW OF VOICE INTERACTION IN GAMES
Natural user interfaces (NUI) have gained popularity re-<re>cently, using gestures, touch, and voice as input methods for
interactive systems [8]. NUIs have been used in the gaming in-<re>dustry to create more immersive experiences, enabling players
to interact with games in new and exciting ways [9]. Human-<re>computer interfaces (HCI) have also been a focus of research
to improve the interaction between humans and computers,
making them more intuitive and user-friendly. Assistive tech-<re>nologies have also been developed to help individuals with
disabilities to interact with games [10].
Accessibility in gaming has become an important area
of research, intending to make games more inclusive and
accessible to individuals with disabilities [11]. Individuals
with mobility impairments primarily utilize speech recognition
software, which allows them to control computers using voice
commands rather than a mouse or keyboard. This technology
enables text entry, command mapping to keyboard macros
(e.g., using Game Commander [12]), and verbal mouse cursor
positioning [13]. Voice interaction has been particularly impor-<re>tant, allowing individuals with limited mobility to play games
without requiring complex physical movements. Additionally,
voice-enabled devices and systems have been used to support
health-related activities, such as exercise and rehabilitation
[14]. For example, voice-activated games have been used in
physical therapy or exercises to improve motor skills and
coordination [15].
Voice interaction is popular for strategy coordination in
online gaming, particularly in FPS games. Wadley et al. [16]
found that voice chat promotes social play and is essential for
MMORPG success. This underscores the importance of intu-<re>itive interfaces like voice interaction for gaming accessibility
and assistive technologies in health-focused games.
In the health-related domain, games mainly relying on voice
interaction are relatively uncommon and often used in the first
scenario examined in our study, where voice-acted characters
speak to the player rather than the opposite [17]. In sports
games like Ring Fit Adventure (Nintendo, 2019), the Ring
character instructs and gives tips to improve the player’s
exercises. In mental health games such as Celeste (Matt
Makes Games, 2018) and Hellblade: Senua’s Sacrifice (Ninja
Theory, 2017), voice-acted characters speak as narrative actors,
using verbal or non-verbal language. In games focused on
patient education, such as Surgeon Simulator (Bossa Studios,
2013) and Two Point Hospital (Two Point Studios and Sega
Europe Ltd., 2018), voice-acted characters make humorous
comments and announcements during gameplay while patients
make noises and scream during surgeries or treatments. In
mental health-focused voice-interaction games like Hellblade
and Sea of Solitude, the game interacts with players through
voice. These games use voice for immersion in mental health
contexts like psychosis, emotional reflection, mindfulness, and
trauma [18]. While voice chat has advantages over text-<re>based communication, it can also negatively impact the player
experience. Unwanted noise and discomfort when playing with
strangers can be common issues.
Allison et al. analyzed over 400 games from platforms
and social media to investigate patterns of voice interaction
[3]. They created a language based on these patterns, exam-<re>ining how voice interaction manifested in relation to game
mechanics. The study highlighted the challenge of “identity
dissonance” [19], which occurs when voice usage conflicts
with the player’s connection to their character, evoking the
question: “Do players speak through or with the character?”.
Finally, dialogue structure patterns examine the arrangement
of speech between the game and the player and the player’s
influence over it [20]. Examples include “Option Selection,”
where players choose from a list of speech options; “Ques-<re>tion and Answer,” resembling virtual assistants like Siri or
Alexa; “Who-What-Where Commands”, involving imperative
commands directed at NPCs; “Scripted Conversation,” similar
to cutscenes where players read character lines; and “Free
Conversation,” allowing players to engage in dialogue without
predetermined questions, closely resembling human-human
dialogue.
III. METHODOLOGY
The study’s methodology commenced with participant pro-<re>file collection, followed by a consistent test script application
for both human participants and generative AIs.
The research initially delved into past impressions of voice
interaction, followed by presenting three scenarios: 1. Game-<re>to-player, 2. Player-to-player, and 3. Player-to-game. Partic-<re>ipants then shared their positive and negative experiences
with voice interaction across these scenarios. Finally, 15 ques-<re>tions centred around these scenarios were administered. More
specifically, they were crafted to mimic prevalent situations in
digital gaming: 1. Game interacts with the player via voice,
2. Player interacts with another player via voice, and 3.
Player interacts with the game via voice. The third scenario
promotes forward-thinking, envisioning currently unattainable
experiences in digital games. Table I displays the distribution
of questions among the scenarios.


Post-interview, conversations were transcribed and stored in
a spreadsheet. The text was analyzed using text mining and
topic identification techniques for qualitative and quantitative
data analysis. Standard measures like means, standard devi-<re>ations, and percentages were employed to evaluate question-<re>naire responses on a Likert scale from 1 (Strongly Disagree) to
5 (Strongly Agree). Additionally, established metrics [21] were
applied to specific questionnaire sections, offering a holistic
view of participants’ experiences and impressions.
A. Participants and Profile Analysis
This study involved a total of 77 human participants,
including 50 game experts from the Brazilian digital game
community (academia and industry) and 27 undergraduate
students from Universidade de Fortaleza, in Brazil. The study
included 5 generative AIs (OpenAI’s ChatGPT 3.5 and 4.0,
Microsoft Bing AI—Creative, Balanced, and Precise—, and
Google Bard). Participants were categorized based on their
profile, with the game experts and undergraduate students
representing the human participant group and the AIs being
the generative participant group.
Out of the 77 human participants, 80% (n = 61) were male,
and 20% (n = 16) were female. When isolating the group of
game experts, 74% (n = 37) were male and 26% (n = 13) were
female. These percentages change considerably when isolating
the group of undergraduate students, with 92% (n = 23) being
male and 8% (n = 2) being female.
Regarding age, 61.04% (n=47) of participants were 20-30
years old, the most represented group, followed by 11.69%
(n=9) aged 20 or younger, with 18 as the youngest. Addition-<re>ally, 15.58% (n=12) were 40-50, 9.09% (n=7) were 30-40, and
2.60% (n=2) were 50 or older, with 58 as the oldest. The game
expert community’s mean age was approximately 30, whereas
the undergraduate student group’s average age was roughly
23.
Of the 50 participants, 71.70% (n=38) had 10 years or
less of experience in game-related studies or work, 16.98%
(n=9) had 10-20 years, 9.43% (n=5) had 20-30 years, and
1.89% (n=1) had 30 or more years. The maximum experience
recorded was 32 years.
B. Interview and Questionnaire
The study involved voluntary interviews with human partic-<re>ipants who accessed a Google Forms survey via a smartphone
QR code. They were typically approached in groups of 3 to
6 and formed impromptu focus groups. After consenting to
participation and interview recording, they proceeded with the
step-by-step completion of the questionnaire.
Human participants engaged in a semi-structured interview
using 15 customized questions (Table I), presented via Google
Forms. Questions were adapted from established user ex-<re>perience evaluation questionnaires (SUS [22], CEGE [21],
SASSI [23]) and the work of [24] for the domain of voice
interaction in digital games. Generative AI participants un-<re>derwent a process similar to human interviews, with a pri-<re>marily textual approach. A detailed explanation of the Likert

each questionnaire section, ensuring consistency with human-<re>participant interactions and maintaining methodological rigour
and quality.
IV. PARTICIPANT INSIGHTS: VOICE INTERACTION IN PAST
DECADES’ GAMES
Among human participants, 64.94% (n=50) agreed that
voice interaction was underexploited in digital games in past
decades, while 35.06% (n=27) disagreed. Interviewees ac-<re>knowledged past technological limitations but also recognized
the increasing prevalence of voice interaction via platforms
like Discord, TeamSpeak, and in-game voice chat systems.
They emphasized the importance of high-quality dubbing for
Brazilian audiences and improvements in the gaming market
due to increased localization efforts. However, they also noted
instances of subpar dubbing, which led to a preference for
original dubbing in some cases, such as in Japanese games.
Voice interaction, where players engage with the game via
voice, has remained underutilized, as observed by Allison et
al. [4]. In the end, participants cited concerns about enjoyment,
given their unfamiliarity with verbally interacting with games
and developers’ preference for traditional peripherals.
In contrast, generative AI participants observed the evolu-<re>tion of voice interaction in games, especially in scenarios 1
and 2. They identified challenges for the third scenario, such
as technological limitations, lack of standardization, imprecise
voice recognition, and difficulty creating immersive voice


interaction. They cited Hey You, Pikachu! as an unsuccessful
example. Some AI participants argued that voice interaction
followed a tide pattern in response to new technologies but
remains less common due to implementation complexity. Over
the past decade, AIs emphasized the growing viability of voice
interaction, driven by advancements in AI and voice recog-<re>nition. Generative AI technologies now facilitate unscripted
NPC interactions. Lastly, AIs emphasized the potential for
more accessible experiences for players with disabilities and
the possibility of designing natural, expressive interactions by
incorporating voice into games.
V. PARTICIPANT PERSPECTIVES ON THE THREE VOICE
INTERACTION SCENARIOS IN DIGITAL GAMING
Based on positive and negative participants’ experiences in
the three voice interaction scenarios, the aim was to explore
their nuances and implications in gaming. Not all human
participants reported experiences in each scenario, but the
Generative AIs did.
A. Scenario 1: Game interacts with the player through voice
Human participants highlighted the importance of voice
acting to overcome language barriers and facilitate content
access. They noted increased investment in game localization
but also cited cases where original audio was preferred due
to translation difficulties. They mentioned Genshin Impact
[25] as an example where translation altered character traits,
impacting the experience. They praised the quality of Japanese
voice acting and cited The Last of Us Part 2’s text-to-<re>speech accessibility feature as an example of game-to-player
voice interaction. Also, some portable consoles have explored
voice interaction in game design through the use of built-<re>in microphones to activate in-game effects. However, the
gaming industry predominantly considers voice interaction
experimental, focusing on traditional input methods.
Similarly, generative AI participants commended story-<re>telling in games like The Last of Us: Part II, Firewatch,
and Hellblade: Senua’s Sacrifice, attributing the heightened
immersion to superior voice acting, dialogue content, and
seamless integration into gameplay. They noted that voice,
as the principal medium for relaying game information, ac-<re>commodates nonverbal auditory cues and offers various con-<re>tent consumption options. AIs highlighted the significance of
companion characters in enhancing gameplay and narrative
experiences but stressed the importance of granting players
control over their involvement. They also cited negative ex-<re>periences in older games like Resident Evil (1996) and Enter
the Matrix (2003) due to subpar audio and dubbing quality.
AIs emphasized the necessity of skillfully produced voices for
effective interpretation and audio in the gaming experience.
B. Scenario 2: Player interacts with another player through
voice
In competitive games like FPS, human participants valued
voice communication for strategy execution but preferred
voice chat with known players. They mentioned games like
Overwatch and Fortnite, using communication systems with
social menus, tactical commands, and pinging systems for
improved gameplay. Participants highlighted that voice quality
and disruptive behaviours significantly affect online gaming.
Issues such as poor microphones, unstable connections, and
harassment negatively impacted gameplay. To address these
issues, they suggested muting harassers and implementing
controls to prevent disruptive behaviour in player-to-NPC
voice interactions. Despite community guidelines and support
initiatives, they acknowledged the challenge of managing
online player behaviour.
Echoing these sentiments, generative AI participants
stressed the value of competitive and cooperative team games,
where voice communication bolsters social presence and im-<re>mersion. Examples include League of Legends, Overwatch,
and Among Us. Players enhance their experience with real-<re>time communication tools during multiplayer matches, consid-<re>ered crucial by the Generative AIs. These games incorporate
social features like emotes or quick messages, seen as less
intrusive and practical for players uncomfortable using their
voices. However, AIs observe that this communication method
is less efficient and authentic than voice interaction, fostering
a more immersive experience. Despite the benefits, most AIs
noted the prevalence of toxic and disruptive behaviour in
multiplayer matches. Players may intentionally intimidate or
exhibit hostility, often through inappropriate comments or
unwelcome noises, discouraging players and hindering coop-<re>eration.
C. Scenario 3: Player interacts with the game through voice
Human participants recognized the gaming industry’s lim-<re>ited focus on voice recognition and natural language pro-<re>cessing technologies due to their insufficient advancement
to justify integration costs. They identified challenges such
as transcription inaccuracies, voice capture quality, ambient
noise, internet speed, and processing power. They emphasized
game design complexities in incorporating voice interaction
and potential dissonance with the player’s identity in RPG
games. A game developer participant cautioned against creat-<re>ing a “virtual slavery” dynamic and raised concerns about the
audience and society shaped by games. Lastly, they envisioned
future advancements in player-to-game voice interaction for
accessibility, enabling players to focus on core gameplay while
using voice commands for secondary aspects.
Corroborating these concerns, generative AI participants
mentioned games like Hey You, Pikachu! and Star Trek:
Bridge Crew as examples of voice interaction in game design.
They emphasized the significance of designing and developing
voice interaction features, enhancing interactivity and immer-<re>sion. However, players might feel uneasy when interacting
with an NPC. AIs also noted the challenge of creating and
maintaining a voice dialogue with NPCs. Games attempting
to implement voice interaction often result in poor experiences
due to inaccurate recognition. AIs identify this issue as a
primary challenge deterring players and developers from uti-<re>lizing voice interaction. They also acknowledged the potential


for enhanced immersion and engagement during cutscenes but
emphasized caution in designing such scenes and interactions
with NPCs.
D. Closing Observations
This section highlights key topics from interview transcripts,
with Figs 1.a and b showcasing words related to discussions,
respectively, with the human participants and generative AIs,
during the questionnaire.
Notably, both humans and AIs emphasize the significance of
“interaction” and “experience” in their respective word clouds,
underlining the shared focus on these aspects. However, while
humans prioritize “dialogue” and “communication” as essen-<re>tial elements, AIs place more importance on “information.”
This distinction may highlight the differing perspectives on
the role of communication in voice interactions, with humans
emphasizing the conversational aspect and AIs focusing on the
information exchange.

VI. COMPREHENSIVE COMPARISONS ASSESSING
PARTICIPANT RESPONSES TO VOICE INTERACTION
SCENARIOS
In this section, we analyze participant feedback from the
questionnaire presented in Table I. Figure 2 compares mean
values and standard deviations (STD) for the 15 questions
answered by all study participants on a 5-point Likert scale.
Positively worded questions (Q1, Q3, Q4, Q6, Q7, Q8, Q9,
Q10, Q11, Q12, Q13, Q14) have a blue background, with
patterns representing game experts, undergraduate students,
and generative AIs. Negatively worded questions (Q2, Q5,
Q15) use a pink background for differentiation.
Tables II, III, and IV show the percentage distribution
of general answers for the three voice interaction scenarios,
with “H” denoting human participants and “AI” representing
generative AI participants. LS stands for Likert Scale.
Human responses revealed positive trends, with mean values
above 3.4, indicating agreement with the question premises.
The descending order of averages, indicating the level of
agreement, is as follows: Q11, Q13, Q8, Q14, Q3, Q1, Q12,
Q4, Q6, and Q7. Conversely, Q9 and Q10 displayed neutral
mean values close to 3. Q9 had the maximum standard
deviation (M = 3.36, STD = 1.34), signifying ambivalence
towards interactive social menus over voice communication.
Potential causes include ambiguous question phrasing or lack
of understanding of interactive social menu functionality. Q8
showed the minimum standard deviation (STD = 0.77), while
Q11 and Q2 had the highest and lowest mean values (M = 4.32
and 2.37, respectively). Human participants partially disagreed
with Q2 (negatively worded), suggesting a limited distinction
between NPC and player-driven character dialogues in reading
or listening experiences.
In this study, undergraduate students exhibited the low-<re>est mean values and highest standard deviations (solid blue
bars), indicating neutral or unfavourable perspectives on voice
interaction in gaming. Conversely, game experts displayed
higher mean values and moderate-to-low standard deviations,
reflecting more consistent opinions among a diverse group.
The human participant results for scenario 1 (“H” columns
in Table II) indicate they view voice positively in digital game
experiences (Q1, M = 4.01, STD = 1.10; Q3, M = 4.05, STD
= 0.99; Q4, M = 3.70, STD = 1.08), often adopting a passive
role, like receiving orders (Q7, M = 3.46, STD = 0.91), not
preferring voice-over text for story consumption (Q5, M =
2.62, STD = 1.12), and following NPC guidance (Q6, M =
3.64, STD = 0.95). They also agree that NPC speech can use
sounds instead of verbal language (Q1, M = 4.01, STD =
1.10) as expressions of NPC behaviours. Regarding concurrent
interaction with a player and an NPC, human participants
recognized a distinction between reading/hearing speech from
NPCs or player-controlled characters (Q2, M = 2.37, STD =
1.10), regardless of whether players or AI control character
expressions. This aligns with Q8 (M = 4.20, STD = 0.76),
where players felt comfortable engaging with NPCs and other
players.
In scenario 2 (“H” columns in Table III), human participants
highlighted voice importance in online matches (Q11, M =
4.32, STD = 1.03), with males agreeing 15.88% more than
females. Voice has become less vital in digital games due to
interactive communication systems like social menus, allowing
for quick character speech but often interrupting gameplay
(Q9, M = 3.31, STD = 1.34). Higher disagreement among
females in this section was expected due to their well-known
unfavourable experiences with male players in online matches
[26]. In Q10 (M = 3.12, STD = 1.27), females agreed with
13.93% more on feeling comfortable using character voices
for in-game communication. Q11 revealed higher agreement
among males (14.96% more), while female results were dis-<re>tributed evenly across agreement, indifference, and disagree-<re>ment.
Finally, in scenario 3 (“H” columns in Table IV), human
participants showed enthusiasm for voice-controlled gameplay,
agreeing on comfort (Q12, M = 3.92, STD = 1.09) and interest
in autonomous voice interaction (Q13, M = 4.22, STD = 1.07).
Some experienced identity dissonance [19] when speaking
through characters with their own voices, potentially impacting
voice acting adoption. Human participants found engaging
with NPCs (Q14, M = 4.11, STD = 1.12) and accessing
narratives unconventionally appealing, being relatively neutral
with NPC tasks being uninteresting (Q15, M = 2.75, STD =
1.29).

For negatively phrased questions Q2, Q5, and Q15, both

In summary, both groups value voice in game experiences,
with humans emphasizing quality and framing while AIs
highlight promptness. Toxic behaviour in online matches is
a concern for human participants, particularly females. Both
groups exhibit enthusiasm for autonomous voice interaction,
but human participants experience identity dissonance when
speaking through characters. AI responses show greater preci-<re>sion, and differences arise in preference for interactive social
menus versus voice communication, with AIs favouring voice
for its immersive and expressive nature.
VII. APPLICATIONS AND FUTURE TRENDS IN GAMES FOR
HEALTH
Our study’s findings link to health game applications and
future trends. By reducing complex interactions to simple
spoken commands, voice interaction can enable quick, context-<re>aware information exchange. For individuals with varying
degrees of visual impairment, voice interaction encompassing
the three scenarios presented in this study offers a wide range
of game design possibilities for accessibility, where voice has
the potential to stand out among existing interaction modalities
and provide new ways to game experience.
Healthcare gaming can benefit from NPCs that allow players
to forge experiences and explore interests in their own words.
Additionally, voice interaction can boost engagement and
inclusivity, especially for disabled individuals, by offering
alternative input methods. The shift towards universal access,
along with the proven efficiency of voice communication, has
been demonstrated by studies such as [16].
With the integration of generative AIs in voice interaction,
we anticipate the development of innovative games that utilize
voice in a myriad of applications, encompassing therapy,
rehabilitation, and promoting a healthy lifestyle. By extending
its impact on health and wellness, voice interaction stands to
transform the landscape of gaming experiences, broadening its
reach and influence in this domain.
VIII. FINAL REMARKS
This investigation delved into the perceptions of voice
interaction within digital games, encompassing a diverse range
of participants, including game experts, undergraduate stu-<re>dents, and generative AIs. The study’s objectives included
augmenting gameplay experiences, addressing disruptive be-<re>haviours, and evaluating the effects of various voice interaction
modalities. In our study, communication in voice interactions
showcases differing perspectives, with humans emphasizing
the conversational aspect and AIs focusing on information
exchange. The findings from the first scenario underscore the


value of incorporating voice interaction in digital games while
emphasizing the crucial role of voice quality and contextual-<re>ization in designing such experiences. The second scenario’s
outcomes reveal the inherent immediacy in voice conversations
yet draw attention to some players’ potential toxicity and dis-<re>ruptive behaviour. Lastly, the third scenario’s results illuminate
the promising future of voice interaction, empowering players
through vocal control while also emphasizing the technical
challenges and uncertainties in integrating this aspect within
game design, given the limited exploration in light of recent
technological advancements.
Regrettably, the gaming industry currently lacks technology
for the third voice interaction scenario presented in this
work. While some games prioritize photorealistic graphics,
emphasizing voice interaction in game development, alongside
conventional input devices, can enhance player experience.
Examining the limitations of current technology can aid in
advancing voice interaction in health applications and inform-<re>ing future gaming trends. Aligned with this initiative, recent
advancements in natural language processing, such as Chat-<re>GPT and Bing Chat, are being integrated with Text-to-Speech
and Speech-to-Text systems for enhanced NPC interactions
in gaming. Ethical and legal factors must be addressed as
these technologies broaden to include image, voice, and sound
generation.
In conclusion, the comparative study revealed that incor-<re>porating voice interactions in digital games effectively capti-<re>vates players, stimulates introspection, and conveys valuable
knowledge. This ultimately contributes to enhanced well-being
and a more immersive gaming experience. As developers
persist in their quest to harness voice technology within the
gaming landscape, innovative solutions may emerge, leading to
increasingly engaging and effective experiences in the health
domain. Future work will explore ethical and practical impli-<re>cations of using AI as participants in voice-based interactions,
focusing on accessibility needs, data sensitivity, and group
dynamics.
